newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa 1996 mergers and acquisitions rise 43 pct.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa 1996 mergers and acquisitions rise 43 pct.

text.p: The value of South African company mergers and acquisitions rose 43 percent to 62.2 billion rand in 1996, driven by unbundling and black empowerment deals, auditing firm Ernst & Young said on Sunday.

The Ernst & Young Annual Survey of Merger & Acquisition Activity said the pace and scale of such deals in 1996 reflected "an economy at an advanced stage in the cyclical upswing, augmented by a business sector undergoing sweeping transformation".

The auditing firm said that 1996 saw a significant increase in the number of large deals valued at more than one billion rand. There were 18 of these "mega-deals" which were valued at 40 billion rand, compared to five such deals in 1995.

The survey said that the 6.1 billion rand restructuring of mining house Anglovaal Ltd's mining interests into two divisions -- diversified mining, development and exploration and gold -- was the largest transaction in the year.

Inward foreign investment was 4.1 billion rand compared to 3.9 billion rand in 1995. One of the largest foreign investments was the acquisition by Malaysian energy group Petronas of 21.6 percent of Engen Ltd for 1.2 billion rand.

Outward investment was six billion rand in 1996 compared to two billion rand in 1995. Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd acquired 11.8 percent of the voting rights of Brazil's Aracruz Celulose SA for 1.12 billion rand.
There were 45 black empowerment deals in 1996 valued at seven billion rand compared with 23 such deals in 1995.
Three black empowerment deals were so-called "mega-deals".

These include African Mining Group's acquisition of 34.9 percent of JCI Ltd for 2.9 billion rand, the 1.6 billion rand restructuring of New Africa Investments Ltd and National Empowerment Consortium's acquisition of 35 percent of Johnnic Ltd for 2.6 billion rand.
The largest unbundling transaction in 1996 was Genbel which was valued at 5.22 billion rand.

"Unbundling and black economic empowerment emerged as major catalysts for mergers and acquisitions activity in 1996, the former accounting for 18 percent and the latter 11 percent of the total transaction value," Ernst & Young said.
